L11@P0: Abstract—Shared virtual memory (SVM) is key in heterogeneous systems on chip (SoCs), which combine a generalpurpose host processor with a many-core accelerator, both for
L12@P0: programmability and to avoid data duplication. However, SVM
L13@P0: can bring a significant run time overhead when translation
L14@P0: lookaside buffer (TLB) entries are missing. Moreover, allowing
L15@P0: DMA burst transfers to write SVM traditionally requires buffers
L16@P0: to absorb transfers that miss in the TLB. These buffers have to
L17@P0: be overprovisioned for the maximum burst size, wasting precious
L18@P0: on-chip memory, and stall all SVM accesses once they are full,
L19@P0: hampering the scalability of parallel accelerators.
L20@P0: In this work, we present our SVM solution that avoids the
L21@P0: majority of TLB misses with prefetching, supports parallel burst
L22@P0: DMA transfers without additional buffers, and can be scaled
L23@P0: with the workload and number of parallel processors. Our
L24@P0: solution is based on three novel concepts: To minimize the rate of
L25@P0: TLB misses, the TLB is proactively filled by compiler-generated
L26@P0: Prefetching Helper Threads, which use run-time information to
L27@P0: issue timely prefetches. To reduce the latency of TLB misses,
L28@P0: misses are handled by a variable number of parallel Miss Handling Helper Threads. To support parallel burst DMA transfers
L29@P0: to SVM without additional buffers, we add lightweight hardware
L30@P0: to a standard DMA engine to detect and react to TLB misses.
L31@P0: Compared to the state of the art, our work improves accelerator
L32@P0: performance for memory-intensive kernels by up to 4× and by
L33@P0: up to 60% for irregular and regular memory access patterns,
L34@P0: respectively.
L35@P0: I. INTRODUCTION
L36@P0: In heterogeneous systems on chip (HeSoCs), a generalpurpose multicore CPU, the host, is co-integrated with programmable many-core accelerators (PMCAs) on a single die.
L37@P0: This design holds the promise of combining the versatility
L38@P0: of the host CPU with the energy efficiency and computing
L39@P0: performance of the highly parallel accelerators.
L40@P0: One of the major difficulties in programming HeSoCs
L41@P0: is having to explicitly manage the multi-level, non-uniform
L42@P0: memory system. On the host, coherent caches and virtual
L43@P0: addresses make the memory hierarchy completely transparent to
L44@P0: the application programmer. On the PMCA, however, scratchpad
L45@P0: memories (SPMs) are often preferred to hardware-managed
L46@P0: caches for the implementation of on-chip memory hierarchies.
L47@P0: SPMs are physically addressed and data transfers to and from
L48@P0: them are controlled by software, preferably using direct memory
L49@P0: access (DMA) transfers.
L50@P0: This work was partially funded by the EU’s H2020 projects HERCULES
L51@P0: (No. 688860) and OPRECOMP (No. 732631).
L52@P0: To alleviate this difficulty and to enable sharing of linked
L53@P0: data structures, the Heterogeneous System Architecture Foundation [1] pushed an architectural model where host and PMCAs
L54@P0: communicate via coherent shared virtual memory (SVM). For
L55@P0: coherency with the host data caches, most SoCs today offer
L56@P0: accelerators access to coherent interconnects [2], [3]. For the
L57@P0: translation of virtual addresses, there are two main approaches:
L58@P0: In the all-hardware approach followed by many embedded
L59@P0: SoC vendors, a full-fledged input/output memory management
L60@P0: unit (IOMMU) translates addresses autonomously [4], [5]. It
L61@P0: is comprised of a translation lookaside buffer (TLB), parallel
L62@P0: hardware page table walkers (PTWs), transaction and data
L63@P0: buffers, and coherent page table caches. The alternative is a
L64@P0: hybrid hardware-software design, which consists of a TLB
L65@P0: controlled by software (e.g., by a kernel driver on the host [6],
L66@P0: [7] or directly by the accelerator [8]). We subsequently refer
L67@P0: to the former class of IOMMUs as conventional and to the
L68@P0: second class as hybrid. While conventional IOMMUs have the
L69@P0: advantage of being transparent to the PMCAs and of offering
L70@P0: the minimal latency for handling an isolated TLB miss, they
L71@P0: have three significant drawbacks:
L72@P0: First, parallel, interleaved accesses by PMCAs to independent
L73@P0: virtual addresses require parallel PTWs. While the number of
L74@P0: parallel accesses is a time-variant run-time property of programs
L75@P0: executed by the PMCAs, the number of PTWs is a fixed design
L76@P0: parameter in conventional IOMMUs. To accommodate a wide
L77@P0: range of parallel workloads, the number of parallel hardware
L78@P0: PTWs must be overprovisioned, wasting hardware resources in
L79@P0: most use cases.
L80@P0: Second, enabling DMA engines to access SVM in conventional IOMMUs requires a data buffer in the IOMMU to absorb
L81@P0: write bursts to addresses that miss in the TLB. This buffer
L82@P0: requires a significant amount of memory: it must have at least
L83@P0: the size of the largest DMA burst, and is usually even larger
L84@P0: because no more SVM accesses (by any master, not just the
L85@P0: missing DMA engine) can be processed once (and as long as)
L86@P0: that buffer is full.
L87@P0: Third, a conventional IOMMU manages its TLB purely
L88@P0: reactively: new entries are set up only after a TLB miss.
L89@P0: While some IOMMUs [9], [5] can speculate on future memory
L90@P0: accesses based on past access patterns, doing so is very inaccurate for nonlinear, interleaved access patterns and negatively
L91@P0-1: arXiv:1808.09751v1 [cs.AR] 29 Aug 2018affects performance [9]. Misses can thus occur frequently,
L92@P1: and high-performance conventional IOMMUs include coherent
L93@P1: data caches for page table entries [5] to reduce the latency of
L94@P1: handling a TLB miss. If the TLB was managed by software
L95@P1: threads in the PMCA instead (as in hybrid IOMMUs), it would
L96@P1: be possible for those threads to set up TLB entries ahead of time
L97@P1: based on run-time information inside the PMCA. Research on
L98@P1: data caches [10], [11] has long shown that prefetchers that know
L99@P1: the running program and its status can be far more accurate
L100@P1: than those that can only see a stream of memory addresses.
L101@P1: The hybrid design, on the other hand, theoretically does not
L102@P1: have these drawbacks. However, the state-of-the-art implementation [8] features only a single PTW thread, only supports
L103@P1: DMA bursts that are guaranteed not to miss (e.g., by locking
L104@P1: the corresponding TLB entries), and does not perform any
L105@P1: prefetching.
L106@P1: In this work, we resolve these limitations. To the best of our
L107@P1: knowledge, this work is the first to:
L108@P1: 1) implement accurate, compiler-generated prefetching for
L109@P1: a shared TLB (§ IV-A), which significantly reduces the
L110@P1: rate of TLB misses,
L111@P1: 2) offer a flexible number of parallel TLB miss handlers
L112@P1: (§ IV-B), which keeps the miss handling latency constant
L113@P1: for scalable parallel workloads, and
L114@P1: 3) offer shared virtual memory accessible by DMA transfers
L115@P1: without additional buffers (§ IV-C).
L116@P1: Compared to the state-of-the-art hybrid IOMMU [8], our
L117@P1: contributions improve the PMCA performance for memoryintensive kernels by up to 4× and by up to 60 % for irregular and
L118@P1: regular memory access patterns, respectively (§V-C). Compared
L119@P1: to using data buffers to absorb bursts from DMA engines, our
L120@P1: solution requires two orders of magnitude less memory (§ V-D)
L121@P1: and scales better, as it only stalls the missing DMA engine.
L122@P1: II. RELATED WORK
L123@P1: The vast majority of commercial systems today features
L124@P1: conventional IOMMUs [5], [12], [13], [14] to completely
L125@P1: abstract the SVM implementation from the PMCAs. While
L126@P1: simple to use, that approach is limited in scalability (handling
L127@P1: parallel misses and absorbing burst transfers) and efficiency
L128@P1: (reactive TLB management).
L129@P1: a) Parallel TLB miss handling and page table walking:
L130@P1: The fixed number of shared hardware PTWs puts an upper
L131@P1: bound on the scalability of conventional IOMMUs to parallel
L132@P1: accelerators. A recent study [9] has shown that an integrated
L133@P1: GPU with 8 parallel compute units (CUs) quickly saturates the
L134@P1: miss handling capabilities of an IOMMU with 16 hardware
L135@P1: PTWs, after which the GPU’s performance becomes bounded by
L136@P1: TLB miss handling latency. To avoid this, the current proposal
L137@P1: for address translation on GPUs [15], [4] is to add one MMU
L138@P1: before the L1 cache in every CU. Each such CU MMU has
L139@P1: its private TLB and either has its own PTW [4] or shares a
L140@P1: highly-threaded PTW [15]. As this approach adds a significant
L141@P1: amount of hardware, its parameters (e.g., TLB size, number
L142@P1: of PTWs) must be carefully balanced at hardware design time
L143@P1: to neither present a bottleneck for SVM-heavy applications
L144@P1: nor reduce the compute-per-area ratio for applications that
L145@P1: use SVM in a lighter way. The miss handling throughput of
L146@P1: hybrid IOMMUs, where page table walks are performed by
L147@P1: software threads, on the other hand, can be scaled at run time by
L148@P1: scheduling PTWs when required. However, efficiently managing
L149@P1: a TLB shared by many parallel processing elements (PEs) and
L150@P1: notifying individual PE with low latency about handled misses
L151@P1: is not trivial. For this reason, current hybrid SVM solutions [8],
L152@P1: [6] only feature a single PTW thread. In this work, we show
L153@P1: how to efficiently manage a shared TLB with multiple software
L154@P1: PTW threads.
L155@P1: b) Handling bursts missing in the TLB: The buffers in
L156@P1: conventional IOMMUs that absorb write bursts missing in the
L157@P1: TLB [5] are another limiting factor for accelerators based on
L158@P1: DMA transfers: When (and as long as) the limit on outstanding
L159@P1: misses is reached, the IOMMU cannot translate any further
L160@P1: transactions, even if they would hit. This creates backpressure
L161@P1: from the IOMMU slave port to the connected master ports,
L162@P1: stalling each master port on its next SVM access. Hybrid
L163@P1: IOMMUs, on the other hand, signal the TLB miss back to
L164@P1: the master and drop the transaction [7]. This allows to handle
L165@P1: misses on a shared TLB in a much more scalable way: instead
L166@P1: of creating congestion on shared resources (e.g., buffers in the
L167@P1: IOMMU, interconnect), the transaction that missed stays in
L168@P1: the source memory, keeping shared resources clear for other
L169@P1: accesses. To support this, the DMA engine must be able to
L170@P1: keep track of bursts that missed and reissue them when the
L171@P1: miss has been handled. In this work, we introduce a lightweight
L172@P1: hardware extension that adds this feature for a standard DMA
L173@P1: engine.
L174@P1: c) Reducing TLB misses through prefetching: Reducing the
L175@P1: number of TLB misses is another effective way to reduce the run
L176@P1: time overhead of SVM, orthogonal to reducing the miss handling
L177@P1: latency. There are two independent strategies to achieve this:
L178@P1: The first is to increase the capacity of the TLB, for which both

L4506@P112: 4.3.6 The DTI-ATS invalidation sequence
L4507@P112: ATS invalidation messages are used only to invalidate ATCs in a PCIe Endpoint. They are not used to invalidate
L4508@P112: TBU caches.
L4509@P112: SMMUv3 requires that a TCU that intends to invalidate entries in an ATC must first invalidate the equivalent TBU
L4510@P112: entries. This results in an invalidation sequence shown in Figure 4-2.
L4511@P112: Figure 4-2 DTI-ATS invalidation sequence
L4512@P112: The invalidation sequence in Figure 4-2 has the following steps:
L4513@P112: 1. The TCU issues a TLB invalidate operation to the TBU and waits for it to complete.
L4514@P112: 2. The TCU issues an invalidation synchronization operation to the TBU and waits for it to complete.
L4515@P112: 3. The TCU issues an ATS invalidation operation to the PCIe Root Complex and waits for it to complete.
L4516@P112: 4. The TCU issues an invalidation synchronization to the PCIe Root Complex and waits for it to complete.
L4517@P112: Note
L4518@P112: In step 3, the DTI_ATS_INV_COMP message is only applicable to DTI-ATSv3 or later version.
L4519@P112: In DTI-ATSv1 and DTI-ATSv2, the return of a DTI_ATS_SYNC_ACK message indicates that:
L4520@P112: • Responses have been received from the appropriate Endpoints for DTI_ATS_INV_REQ messages that were
L4521@P112: received before the corresponding DTI_ATS_SYNC_REQ was received.

L4539@P113: In DTI-ATSv3 or later, the return of a DTI_ATS_SYNC_ACK message instead indicates that:
L4540@P113: • No further accesses to memory are made using translations invalidated by DTI_ATS_INV_REQ messages

L4542@P113: Note
L4543@P113: A DTI_ATS_SYNC_ACK message is likely to be dependent on completion of outstanding translations in the
L4544@P113: downstream TBU. This does not cause deadlocks because SMMUv3 stalling faults are not permitted for PCIe RPs.
L4545@P113: This dependency is likely because DTI_ATS_SYNC_ACK depends on the Root Complex receiving invalidation
L4546@P113: completion messages from Endpoints, and those completion messages are ordered behind posted writes that might
L4547@P113: need translating.
L4548@P113: Handling outstanding invalidations
L4549@P113: PCIe requires that Endpoints support a minimum of 32 outstanding invalidation operations that must be accepted
L4550@P113: whether downstream transactions are able to make forward progress or not.
L4551@P113: However, not all Endpoints can consume this number of invalidation operations without back pressure. For
L4552@P113: performance reasons, the number of invalidate operations that should be outstanding in an Endpoint at one time
L4553@P113: might be less.
L4554@P113: A PCIe RPs indicates in DTI_ATS_CONDIS_REQ.TOK_INV_GNT how many invalidation messages it can accept
L4555@P113: without giving back pressure on the DTI interface. It should buffer these locally so that the DTI interface is not
L4556@P113: stalled waiting for an Endpoint to progress an invalidation.
L4557@P113: DTI-ATS invalidation tokens are only used for flow control of invalidation messages on the DTI channel. The Root
L4558@P113: Complex does not need to receive an Invalidation Completion message from an Endpoint before it returns a
L4559@P113: DTI_ATS_INV_ACK message on DTI-ATS. It can return a DTI_ATS_INV_ACK message as soon as it has
L4560@P113: successfully sent an Invalidation Request message to the Endpoint and is able to buffer a new DTI_ATS_INV_REQ
L4561@P113: message.
L4562@P113: The Endpoint must return all Invalidation Completion messages before the Root Complex returns a
L4563@P113: DTI_ATS_SYNC_ACK message. If a new DTI_ATS_INV_REQ message is received after a
L4564@P113: DTI_ATS_SYNC_REQ, the Root Complex must do both of the following:
L4565@P113: • Issue an Invalidation Request message to the Endpoint without waiting for the DTI_ATS_SYNC_ACK to be
L4566@P113: returned.
L4567@P113: • Not wait for a corresponding Invalidation Completion message from the Endpoint for this invalidation before
L4568@P113: returning the currently outstanding DTI_ATS_SYNC_ACK message.
L4569@P113: Ensuring downstream transaction completion
L4570@P113: When an Endpoint returns an Invalidation Completion message, it guarantees that:
L4571@P113: • All outstanding read requests that use the invalidated translations are complete.
L4572@P113: • All posted write requests are pushed ahead of the Invalidation Completion message.
L4573@P113: It does not guarantee that the posted write requests are complete, as memory writes in PCIe do not receive a
L4574@P113: response.
L4575@P113: To ensure correct ordering, the Root Complex must ensure that posted writes intended for the AMBA system that
L4576@P113: were received before the Invalidation Completion, have been issued downstream and are complete. A Root
L4577@P113: Complex can only return a DTI_ATS_SYNC_ACK message when this requirement has been met. The Root
L4578@P113: Complex is not required to ensure that reads are complete because this has already been ensured by the Endpoint.

L1721@P46: 4.2 Traffic Classes
L1722@P46: Intel DSA includes support for Traffic Classes as defined in PCIe, if the PCIe VC capability is present.
L1723@P46: Traffic Classes may be used by the platform outside of the device to control QoS for memory
L1724@P46: transactions initiated by the device.
L1725@P46: Traffic Classes are also used within the device to segregate traffic destined for low bandwidth memory.
L1726@P46: Each platform has one or more designated traffic class values that should be used for accesses to low
L1727@P46: bandwidth memory. See section 4.5 for information on configuring traffic classes for use with low
L1728@P46: bandwidth memory.
L1729@P46: There are two traffic class registers in each Group Configuration register. Traffic Classes specified in the
L1730@P46: Group Configuration traffic class registers must have valid mappings in the TC/VC Maps in the PCIe
L1731@P46: Virtual Channel Extended Capability structure. Each descriptor has flags to select which of the two
L1732@P46: traffic classes to use for each address used by the descriptor. For best results, software should ensure
L1733@P46-47: that operations with dissimilar QoS characteristics are issued to different groups.Intel® Data Streaming Accelerator Architecture Specification

L1736@P47: 4.3 Read Buffer Allocation
L1737@P47: The Intel DSA device uses read buffers to hide memory read latency. Software can control how these
L1738@P47: read buffers are allocated, which affects the read bandwidth available to certain guests or applications.
L1739@P47: Read Buffers are resources within the Intel DSA implementation that are allocated to engines to support
L1740@P47: memory read operations. The total number of Read Buffers supported is fixed by the implementation
L1741@P47: and is reported in the GRPCAP register. Limiting the number of Read Buffers available to a group can
L1742@P47: restrict the read bandwidth usable by engines in the group. The relationship between Read Buffers and
L1743@P47: actual bandwidth is dependent on instantaneous system memory latency and varies dynamically as
L1744@P47: system utilization changes. Read Buffers are internal to the design of Intel DSA and are not related to
L1745@P47: other resources in the SoC that also affect the bandwidth available to the device.
L1746@P47: The policy by which Read Buffers are allocated to groups is based on two fields in the Group
L1747@P47: Configuration registers. The Read Buffers Reserved field indicates the number of Read Buffers set aside
L1748@P47: for the exclusive use of engines in the group. The Read Buffers Allowed field indicates the maximum
L1749@P47: number of Read Buffers that may be in use at one time by all engines in the group. (Read Buffers
L1750@P47: allocated to a group may also be limited by the Global Read Buffer Limit, as described in section 9.2.8.)
L1751@P47: Setting the Read Buffers Reserved field to a non-zero value ensures that engines in the group are able
L1752@P47: to acquire Read Buffers without being starved by engines in other groups. However, reserving Read
L1753@P47: Buffers for a group limits the number of Read Buffers available to other groups, potentially limiting their
L1754@P47: ability to efficiently utilize the bandwidth capability of the device. The sum of the Read Buffers reserved
L1755@P47: for all groups must be no greater than the total number of Read Buffers available (as reported in
L1756@P47: GRPCAP).
L1757@P47: For each group, the Read Buffers Allowed field must be greater than or equal to 4 times the number of
L1758@P47: engines in the group. It must also be no greater than the value of the Read Buffers Reserved field for that
L1759@P47: group plus the number of non-reserved Read Buffers. The number of non-reserved Read Buffers is
L1760@P47: defined as the total number of Read Buffers supported minus the number of Read Buffers reserved for
L1761@P47: all groups combined. For example, if the device supports 74 Read Buffers and 3 are reserved for each of
L1762@P47: the four groups, then 62 Read Buffers remain non-reserved, and the maximum value of Read Buffers
L1763@P47: Allowed for each group would be 65.
L1764@P47: There is a system-specific value for the Read Buffers Allowed field (dependent on the read latency of
L1765@P47: the system) that allows the group to utilize the full bandwidth of the device. This value can be calibrated
L1766@P47: by software. There is no advantage to setting the Read Buffers Allowed field to a greater value. Setting
L1767@P47: this field to a smaller value limits the Read Buffers that can be allocated to engines in the group, thereby
L1768@P47: limiting their impact on the performance of engines in other groups.
L1769@P47: 4.4 Latency Control
L1770@P47: Intel DSA provides controls for software to reduce the latency impact of multiple outstanding
L1771@P47: descriptors being in progress in the device. Within an engine, multiple descriptors may be processed
L1772@P47: concurrently, in a pipelined manner. If the Descriptors in Progress Limit Supported field in GRPCAP is 1,
L1773@P47: the Maximum Work Descriptors in Progress and Maximum Batch Descriptors in Progress fields in
L1774@P47: ENGCAP specify the maximum number that may be concurrently in process in an engine at a given time.
